# Summary of John L. Pollock
John L. Pollock (1940–2009) was an influential American philosopher renowned for his work in epistemology, philosophical logic, and artificial intelligence. Pollock made foundational contributions to the philosophy of defeasible reasoning, earning him the informal title "Mr. Defeasible Reasoning." His 1987 paper "Defeasible reasoning" and his book "Knowledge and Justification" were critical in bringing the concept into mainstream philosophy, distinguishing key defeat mechanisms such as "undercutting defeat" and "rebutting defeat." He traced the origins of his thinking to his 1967 paper "Criteria and our knowledge of the material world," and acknowledged influences such as Roderick Chisholm, Ludwig Wittgenstein, and Stephen Toulmin.
Beyond his theoretical work, Pollock developed OSCAR, a LISP-based artificial intelligence system designed to embody his theories on defeasible reasoning and implement cognitive features like interest-driven reasoning, planning, and problem-solving strategies. He also contributed broadly to epistemology with works such as "Knowledge and Justification" and investigated the foundations of probability and induction in his book "Nomic Probability and the Foundations of Induction." Pollock served on faculties at several universities, notably the University of Arizona, where he helped found the Cognitive Science Program, and published extensively on topics including logic, probability, reasoning, and rational decision-making.
